questions.stem: Which one-word substitution correctly describes a person who collects and studies coins?

options.option_text: Philatelist — one who collects postage stamps
Numismatist — one who collects and studies coins
Bibliophile — one who loves collecting books
Cartographer — one who makes or draws maps

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Numismatist' is formed from Greek 'nomisma' (coin) + Latin '-ist' (practitioner/specialist); the study itself is called 'numismatics'. Word-formation rule: the suffix '-ist' attaches to a noun root to name the person who practises or studies that thing (e.g., botanist, economist). Common trap: Philatelist also ends in '-ist' and names a collector, but its root is Greek 'philos' (loving) + 'ateleia' (exemption from tax — early stamps bore that mark), so it refers to stamp-collecting, not coins.

questions.stem: Choose the correct one-word substitution for a person who walks around while fast asleep.

options.option_text: Insomniac — a person who habitually cannot fall asleep
Narcoleptic — a person prone to sudden uncontrollable sleep
Somniloquist — a person who talks aloud while fast asleep
Somnambulist — a person who walks about while in deep sleep

questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Somnambulist' = Latin 'somnus' (sleep) + 'ambulare' (to walk) + '-ist' (person). Word-formation rule: compound Latin roots describe the activity precisely — somnus appears in 'insomnia' (in- = not, so no sleep) and ambu­lare appears in 'ambulance' (vehicle that moves/walks). The sharpest trap is C: 'Somniloquist' shares the 'somn-' root but pairs it with 'loqui' (to speak), making it someone who TALKS in sleep, not walks. Example applying the same root rule: 'perambulator' = per (through) + ambulare = a pram that 'walks' a baby around.

questions.stem: Identify the one-word substitution for a person who believes that God's existence can neither be proved nor disproved.

options.option_text: Agnostic — one who holds that God's existence is unknowable
Atheist — one who firmly and completely denies God's existence
Theist — one who firmly believes in the existence of a deity
Deist — one who accepts God but rejects organised religious doctrine

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Agnostic' = Greek prefix 'a-' (without/not) + 'gnosis' (knowledge) — literally 'one without knowledge' about God's existence. Word-formation rule: the privative prefix 'a-/an-' negates the root (e.g., amoral, atypical, anonymous). The classic exam trap is B — Atheist (Greek 'a-' + 'theos' = god) goes further by actively DENYING God's existence, whereas an Agnostic merely claims certainty is impossible. Another example of this 'a-' pattern: 'Anarchist' = a- + archos (ruler) = one who rejects all rulers.

questions.stem: Which word correctly substitutes the phrase 'the act of killing one's own father'?

options.option_text: Fratricide — the act of killing one's own brother
Filicide — the act of a parent deliberately killing their child
Patricide — the act of killing one's own father
Regicide — the act of killing a reigning monarch or king

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Patricide' = Latin 'pater/patris' (father) + '-cide' (killing, from 'caedere'). Word-formation rule: the suffix '-cide' always denotes killing and attaches to a Latin noun identifying the victim. Full family: Fratricide (frater = brother), Matricide (mater = mother), Uxoricide (uxor = wife), Filicide (filius = son/child), Regicide (rex/regis = king), Infanticide (infans = infant). Memory hook: PATRiarch, PATRiot, PATRimony all share the 'patr-' root meaning father — PAT­ricide turns that root violent.

questions.stem: A person who lives entirely by begging is best described by which one-word substitution?

options.option_text: Mendicant — a person who lives entirely by seeking alms
Vagrant — a person who wanders without any fixed home
Recluse — a person who withdraws and lives in strict isolation
Nomad — a person who roams from place to place seasonally

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Mendicant' = Latin 'mendicare' (to beg) + '-ant' (agent suffix meaning 'one who does'). Word-formation rule: '-ant' creates agent nouns from verbs (e.g., 'supplicant' from supplicare = to kneel/plead). The common confusion is with 'Vagrant' (Latin vagari = to wander), which stresses homelessness/wandering, not begging; a vagrant may not beg. Historical note: Mendicant Friars (Franciscans, Dominicans) took vows of poverty and begged for sustenance — this is a high-frequency PYQ angle. Warning: 'Mendacious' (lying) looks similar but comes from 'mendax' (liar), a completely different root.

questions.stem: Which word correctly denotes an excessive and irrational fear of open or public spaces?

options.option_text: Claustrophobia — an intense fear of enclosed or confined spaces
Acrophobia — an intense fear of heights and elevated places
Agoraphobia — an intense fear of open or crowded public spaces
Xenophobia — an intense fear or hatred of foreign people

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Agoraphobia' = Greek 'agora' (open marketplace, the civic centre of ancient Greek cities) + 'phobia' (fear). Word-formation rule: all '-phobia' compounds follow the pattern Greek noun + '-phobia'; the root names the feared object/situation. The number-one exam trap is A — Claustrophobia (Latin 'claustrum' = bolt/enclosed space) is the precise OPPOSITE: fear of confined spaces. Mnemonic: AGORA = open public square (think 'aggregate' = gather together publicly) → Agoraphobia = fear of open/public gathering spaces. Other '-phobia' words SSC tests: Hydrophobia (water), Nyctophobia (night/darkness), Dendrophobia (trees).

questions.stem: Select the one-word substitution for a formal speech of praise delivered in honour of a deceased person.

options.option_text: Elegy — a mournful poem written to lament someone who has died
Epitaph — an inscription carved on a gravestone for the deceased
Obituary — a published notice briefly announcing someone's death
Eulogy — a formal speech delivering praise for a deceased person

questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Eulogy' = Greek 'eu-' (well/good) + 'logos' (word/speech) — literally 'speaking well (of someone)'. Word-formation rule: the prefix 'eu-' means 'well/good' and appears in Euphoria (eu + phora = good feeling), Euphemism (eu + pheme = good speech), Euthanasia (eu + thanatos = good death). Three sharply distinct traps: (1) Elegy — a POEM of mourning, not a speech of praise (Greek elegos = a song of mourning); (2) Epitaph — a WRITTEN INSCRIPTION on a tomb (Greek epi = upon + taphos = tomb); (3) Obituary — a factual NEWSPAPER NOTICE of death listing achievements, not a live tribute speech. The key discriminator: Eulogy is always SPOKEN and always PRAISES.
